The record:
Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: HighErrorRate on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: Error rate above threshold for 5m {A1}
Alert raised: 2026-11-11T03:43:30Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged. Argus first posted about the incident in Slack at 2026-11-11T03:43:53Z {first_told}, and the document says so already: leave that post out, and do not say that no person was told. That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule waits 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires. The alert came within the 7 minutes 30 seconds {accounted_for} accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute {rule_evaluated_every}, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds {scraping_allowance} for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute the onset is measured to.
Broken from 2026-11-11T03:37:00Z {began} (the onset, dated to its minute: a change came during that minute) to 2026-11-11T03:49:00Z {back_to_normal}, when the metrics show it back to normal.
That is 12 minutes {duration}, and every impact figure below is measured over that stretch.
Argus held the incident for 6 minutes 20 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-11T03:50:12Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
The service's error rate over all its requests, before it began: 1.1% {errors_before}.
The same rate while it was broken: 29.2% {errors_while_broken}, peaking at 33.5% {errors_at_worst}.
Rise above baseline: 28.1% {errors_rise} of traffic failed that otherwise would not have.
The series behind the alert, `sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[1m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[1m]))` - its alert said "Error rate above threshold for 5m {A1}" - which its alert rule evaluates and calls worse rising: 1.0750000000000001% {series_before} before it began, 29.20833333333333% {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 33.5% {series_at_worst} at its worst. Say what it measures in words, not by its query.
Customer loss: 8,013.46 USD {customer_loss} - how far the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier, beyond how much those hours vary on their own.

A person's message never stops a step already running: between steps, Argus starts no new one while a message waits to be answered.

Changes to production it read:
  - [P1] 2026-11-11T03:37:13Z {P1.1} flag-toggle legacy-checkout-fallback by admin: feature flag legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off
  - [P2] 2026-11-11T03:37:13Z {P2.1} flag-toggle monthly-spend-feature by admin: feature flag monthly-spend-feature was switched on
  - Deploys read, none came back.

Log lines it read, one per message:
  - [G153f] INFO io-shop: legacy-checkout-fallback=on - 200 {G153f.1} evaluations - 1 {G153f.2} occurrence in 1 {G153f.3} minute, 03:36 {G153f.4}
  - [G7e5d] INFO io-shop: monthly-spend-feature=off - 200 {G7e5d.1} evaluations - 1 {G7e5d.2} occurrence in 1 {G7e5d.3} minute, 03:36 {G7e5d.4}

  - [G5309] ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ZeroDivisionError: division by zero at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47 - 13 {G5309.1} occurrences in 7 {G5309.2} minutes, 03:37–03:43 {G5309.3}
  - [G7037] INFO io-shop: legacy-checkout-fallback=off - 200 {G7037.1} evaluations - 6 {G7037.2} occurrences in 6 {G7037.3} minutes, 03:38–03:43 {G7037.4}
  - [Gce95] INFO io-shop: monthly-spend-feature=on - 200 {Gce95.1} evaluations - 6 {Gce95.2} occurrences in 6 {Gce95.3} minutes, 03:38–03:43 {Gce95.4}

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - name them by their labels, but cite none; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1] Feature flag monthly-spend-feature was switched on at 2026-11-11T03:37:13Z {C1.1}. The new spend-summary path then raised ZeroDivisionError at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47, and the error rate stepped from about 1% {C1.2} to about 30% {C1.3}. No deployment occurred and the rollout had converged. [feature-flag-toggle, confidence 0.6 {C1.4}, refuted]
  - [C2] Feature flag legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off at 2026-11-11T03:37:13Z {C2.1}. Account pages moved from the legacy renderer to the new renderer, which hits the failing spend_summary code path. This flag toggled at the same instant as monthly-spend-feature, so the logs cannot separate the two. [feature-flag-toggle, confidence 0.35 {C2.2}, confirmed]

Actions it took:
  - [M1] Reverted the feature flag monthly-spend-feature for [C1] (can be put back) - refuted, put back when it did not help
  - [M2] Reverted the feature flag legacy-checkout-fallback for [C2] (can be put back) - confirmed, still in place

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] The fault: in `src/io_shop/spend_summary.py`, `average_spend_per_item_this_month` returns `account.total_this_month_cents // len(bought_this_month)`. That is line 47 {F1.1}, the line named in the ZeroDivisionError the investigation logged. `bought_this_month` is the list of purchases with `in_current_month` set, so it is empty for any shopper who has not bought anything this month. The test file's own fixture calls that "the ordinary case". `render_spend_summary` sends every request with `use_monthly_summary` on to this function. So every account page served through that path for an idle-this-month shopper raised, and `serve_account_page` in `src/io_shop/account_page.py` turned each one into a failed page. Unlike the lifetime average's empty divisor, which only a shopper with no history at all can reach, this is an input real shoppers bring every day. So it is a code fault no matter which flag or renderer change exposed it, and turning the flag back off only hid it.
      
      The change: when there are no purchases this month, the function returns 0 {F1.2}, which is what the shopper has spent per item this month. Otherwise it divides as before. Nothing is swallowed: no exception is caught, and the empty case is handled by checking for it. `render_spend_summary` and its caller `_the_figure_for` still get an `int`, as their signatures expect. The lifetime average `average_spend_per_item` is untouched. It still raises for an account with no purchases at all, and the existing tests in `tests/io_shop/test_account_page.py` and `tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py` depend on that, including the check that the line they name contains `//`.
      
      The test: `tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py` gains two cases. One calls `average_spend_per_item_this_month` on a shopper with lifetime purchases but none this month. The other goes through `render_spend_summary(..., use_monthly_summary=True)`. Both assert the figure is 0 {F1.3}. Against the current code, both would raise ZeroDivisionError.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'.

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, done): Reverted the feature flag legacy-checkout-fallback
  - AI-2 (prevent, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
PR #549 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.
The document already states what set it off, in a section of its own: the change [P1].

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

What people working the incident wrote in its thread:
  - L1 (Some Person, 2026-11-11T03:44:39Z): "it's legacy-checkout-fallback - someone switched it off right before this started" - the investigation found it unverified: legacy-checkout-fallback did switch off at 03:37:13Z, but monthly-spend-feature was switched on at the same instant and the errors are ZeroDivisionError in spend_summary.py:47, which points at the spend feature. The two flags moved in lockstep, so the logs cannot separate them.
Each was weighed on what the investigation had read, before anything was tried. Where the actions above say otherwise, the actions are the later word.
For each, say in lead_effects whether it changed what was done.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

The document, by field:
root_cause: With legacy-checkout-fallback off, account pages took a path where `average_spend_per_item_this_month` in `src/io_shop/spend_summary.py` divides the month's total by the number of purchases this month. That list is empty for any shopper who has bought nothing this month, so the division raised ZeroDivisionError at line 47, and `serve_account_page` turned each one into a failed page. It rests on F1, a reading of the source nothing ran, so it is unverified.
cause_in_plain_words: An administrator switched off an older fallback for showing shoppers their account pages, which sent those pages through newer code that most likely breaks when it works out a shopper's average spend for the month if they have bought nothing that month.
still_at_risk: If anyone switches legacy-checkout-fallback off again, account pages could fail again for shoppers who have bought nothing this month.
symptom: Shoppers' account pages failed to load
lead_effects L1: It did not change what was done: the investigation weighed it as unverified and reverted monthly-spend-feature first, and reverted legacy-checkout-fallback, the flag the lead named, only after the first action was refuted; that revert was confirmed, so the lead proved right.
causal_chain 1: Shoppers' account page requests failed: the error rate on account pages went up and stayed up. (cites Gbac1, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; G5309, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 2: The failing account page requests raised ZeroDivisionError at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47. (cites G5309, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 3: Account pages were no longer served by the legacy renderer. The new renderer served them instead, and that path reaches the failing spend-summary code. This followed legacy-checkout-fallback reading off in the flag evaluations. (cites Gc27d, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; G7ad6, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; G7037, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; T29, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 4: An admin switched feature flag legacy-checkout-fallback off. (cites P1, under "Changes to production it read")
causal_chain 4 ruled_out 1: Feature flag monthly-spend-feature, which the same admin switched on at the same instant: turning it back off left the service at the incident's level, so it was put back. (cites T20, under "What Argus did, in order"; T22, under "What Argus did, in order"; T23, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 5: On that path, the spend summary divides the month's total by the number of purchases this month, and that list is empty for any shopper who has bought nothing this month. (cites F1, under "What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix")
contributing_factors 1: No staged rollout or automatic guard was seen on the flag change. legacy-checkout-fallback went from on to off for all account page traffic within the minute it was switched.
contributing_factors 1 had_it_been_otherwise: A staged switch that watched the error rate would have stopped at a small share of shoppers and switched back, before most account pages failed.
contributing_factors 2: No check was seen that exercised the code path a flag switch turns on before the switch was made in production. Here that path was the new renderer's spend summary for a shopper with no purchases this month.
contributing_factors 2 had_it_been_otherwise: The division fault would have shown up before the flag was switched, and the switch would not have gone out.
contributing_factors 3: Two flags on the same service were switched by the same admin at the same instant, so the logs could not separate their effects.
contributing_factors 3 had_it_been_otherwise: With the flags changed one at a time, the errors would have lined up with the one change that caused them, and the right flag could have been reverted first, shortening the incident.
contributing_factors 4: Nobody was paged when the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop fired: no on-call incident was linked to this one.
contributing_factors 4 had_it_been_otherwise: A person would have been brought in when the alert fired, able to weigh the leads alongside Argus and step in if the automated response went wrong.
action_items 1: Put flag changes on io-shop behind a staged rollout that widens step by step and switches back on its own when the account page error rate rises.
action_items 2: Before any flag switch goes to production, run tests that exercise the code path the switch turns on, including shoppers with no purchases in the current month.
action_items 3: Require flag changes on the same service to go out one at a time, with the service checked between them.
action_items 4: Find out why no on-call person was paged for the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop, and make sure it pages one when it fires.
went_well 5: Every action taken was a flag revert that could be put back.
went_wrong 1: The response acted first on monthly-spend-feature, the higher-ranked candidate, even though the person's lead named legacy-checkout-fallback. That revert did not help, and account pages kept failing until the second flag was reverted.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {T5.1} or {duration}, are figures code writes in from the row they name. They are not judged.
  - Action items propose what to do; they make no claim about the record.
  - Whether something went well, went wrong or was lucky is a judgement. Only a fact it states is judged.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
